title: Salve Regina

segments.voice: Yesterday, Regina Caeli: the Easter prayer, he is risen, as he said, with an alleluia on every line. Your line was queen of heaven, rejoice. Which promise did you keep? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-eight.

A valley of tears. It's a strange address to put in a prayer, and an honest one. After the feasts are over, after Easter and Pentecost, the Church settles into the long green stretch of the year it calls Ordinary Time. No big feast most weeks. Just Mondays, laundry, work, a sick parent, a good dinner, a bad night. And for that stretch, the song at the end of night prayer is the one that knows exactly where we live. It begins with a greeting, hail, holy queen, and before it's done it has named exile, sighing, mourning and weeping. Today's word is the antiphon of ordinary days: Salve Regina.
screen: `A VALLEY OF TEARS.` → `THE LONG GREEN STRETCH: ORDINARY TIME.` → `A SONG FOR ORDINARY DAYS.`

segments.voice: It moves in four steps. First, names, one after another: Salve Regina, mater misericordiae. Hail, queen, mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope. Life, sweetness, hope: large words, said in a single breath. Second, the truth about where the singers stand. To you we cry, it says, exiled children of Eve. To you we send up our sighs, mourning and weeping in this valley of tears. A few days ago we met Mary as the new Eve, who untied the knot. Here the singers call themselves Eve's children, still far from home. The prayer doesn't pretend that ordinary life is easy. It names the tears and keeps singing. Third, the request. Turn your eyes of mercy toward us, it asks, and after this exile, show us Jesus, the blessed fruit of your womb. That phrase comes from Elizabeth's greeting in Luke's Gospel, which the Douay-Rheims gives as "blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Notice what the prayer asks Mary for: not to stand in for her son, but to show him. The whole song leans toward him. Fourth, three last cries: O clemens, O pia, O dulcis Virgo Maria. O clement, O loving, O sweet Virgin Mary. A story people tell links those last cries to Saint Bernard of Clairvaux; it isn't certain. Either way, the song ends not with an argument but with a sigh of affection. Hail, holy queen, on an ordinary night, in an ordinary valley, with the lights about to go out.
screen: `MOTHER OF MERCY, OUR LIFE, OUR HOPE.` · `EXILED CHILDREN OF EVE, IN TEARS.` · `SHOW US JESUS.` · `O CLEMENT, O LOVING, O SWEET.` · then, large: `BLESSED IS THE FRUIT OF THY WOMB.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing or say it tonight. Now, a rehearsal. Settle, and breathe. Name, quietly and honestly, one thing in your valley right now. Something heavy you've been carrying through ordinary days. Don't dress it up. Then name one sweetness that's also true: a person, a small joy, a reason for hope. Hold both, side by side, the way the prayer does. Tonight, before sleep, if you pray, you can say or sing the Salve Regina, from hail, holy queen to O sweet Virgin Mary. If you don't, let the day end by naming the same two things again: one tear, one hope. The bell holds the time.
Salve Regina. Hail, holy queen: the night song of Ordinary Time, honest about the valley of tears, asking to be shown Jesus. Today's word.
Your line: hail, holy queen. Today, when someone asks how you are, give one honest answer, the tear and the hope both. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics sing or say the Salve Regina at the end of Night Prayer in Ordinary Time, and it is also prayed at the end of the rosary; some religious communities sing it together in chant before the night's silence.

notes: The English of the Salve Regina is given unquoted, close to the traditional English ('Hail, holy Queen, Mother of mercy, our life, our sweetness and our hope...'). The traditional English is old, but its translation is not on the validator's public-domain list, so it is not marked as a quotation. Confirm.
Season: traditionally from Trinity Sunday (after Pentecost) until Advent; the current Liturgy of the Hours also allows it at other times. The script says 'for that stretch', per the index. Confirm.
Attribution of the final 'O clemens, O pia, O dulcis' to Bernard of Clairvaux given only as 'a story people tell; nobody can prove it'.
howItsDone says it is prayed at the end of the rosary; confirm phrasing ('often').
Callback to day 1329 (the new Eve) refers to 'a few days ago'.

Editor pass: 'three last cries, each shorter than the one before' corrected (the last, O dulcis Virgo Maria, is the longest); 'piled up like a child who can't stop' cut, since day 1332 already used the child's pile of names; 'nobody can prove it' softened to 'it isn't certain'.
